textContent.text: Ezra McBride had big dreams. His father was a legend, known for finding gold where others found only dust and rocks. Ezra wanted to be just as good.
It was all he could talk about. Every free moment, he walked around the family's California ranch. He dug through dirt and even inspected the barn.
But Ezra's luck seemed as dry as the land around him.
One morning, as Ezra walked to the schoolhouse, a new girl ran up beside him. "My name's Jesse," she announced. "I just moved to town."
In her arms, Jesse carried a stack of maps and books. Ezra noticed that they were all about local rivers, hills, and mineral deposits.
Jesse continued, "I heard you like looking for gold. Want some help?"
Ezra shook his head. He didn't need help from someone who had only been here for a few days. His dad was the best miner around.

"I might just surprise you," Jesse said, grinning. "I may be new, but I've got a few ideas that might help you." Jesse opened a book and an old map. "It looks like a river used to run across your family's land. What if we try digging there?"
"Listen. I know my home better than you. You can search with me, but we do it my way."
Jesse shrugged. "I guess that's the way it's got to be," she said. After school, they walked along the dusty road toward the McBride farm.

In the days that followed, Ezra took them to a handful of promising spots. But time after time they uncovered nothing but rocks and dead bushes. Ezra started to wonder if he was being stubborn. Jesse's ideas couldn't be any worse than his.
One day, on the walk back from school, Ezra said. "Say, Jesse. Remember that old river you talked about? What do you say we give it a try?"
Jesse smiled at Ezra and nodded. "Yes!"

Hours later, Ezra spotted a few shiny flakes of gold right where Jesse thought they might be. Then, as he dug through more dirt, Ezra's heart beat faster. There were even small gold nuggets in the dirt.
He couldn't believe it. Jesse and her maps had guessed right.
Ezra leapt up. He grabbed Jesse's arms and spun them in a circle. "Jesse, you did it! You knew just where to look. We're going to be California legends, just like my dad!"

"Computer, run a check on the crystal," she commanded.
A screen blinked to life. "Warning: Crystal health at 70%. Crack detected," the ship's computer announced.

Captain Flores raced back to her office. She had to figure out how to fix the crystal. She pulled out a dusty repair book, and flipped through the pages. "We have to push through anyways," she huffed. But her eyes fell on the first rule in the repair book.
"Safety is the most important thing. The crew and ship must be taken care of before everything else," she read slowly.
Captain Flores sighed. She stood up and headed towards the cafeteria, calling a meeting over the ship's speakers. She knew what she had to do.

"Safety is the most important thing. The crew and ship must be taken care of before everything else," she read slowly.

textContent.text: Jamal whipped his arm forward to throw a baseball toward home plate. It clanged against the metal fence and rolled through the dirt in the empty baseball field. Now that his best friend Nico had moved away, Jamal had no one to practice throwing with.

Jamal kept coming to the baseball field after Nico left, but it wasn't the same. Nico was the only person Jamal knew who loved baseball as much as he did. Other kids wanted to play something else after twenty minutes of tossing a baseball. But Jamal and Nico had thrown for hours, pretending to be their favorite pitcher, Mario Rodríguez.

"That would be a lot easier if you had a catcher," Jamal heard, bringing his attention back to the field. The words came from a boy Jamal didn't know. The boy walked to home plate, picked up the ball, and tossed it back to Jamal.
"Yeah, I guess," said Jamal as he stood on the mound. Here was another kid who would probably play for ten minutes before suggesting a different game.
The boy strolled toward him. "My name's Zeke. My family just moved here for my dad's job." Zeke pointed at the shirt Jamal was wearing. "I like your Rodríguez jersey."
"Thanks," Jamal said with a shrug. He tossed the ball into his glove a few times.

pieces.text: "Check this out," said Zeke. He held up a well-used baseball glove and pointed to an autograph on the palm. Jamal read it aloud: "

textContent.text: Jamal's mouth hung open. "Wait! You met M-Rod?" he said. He rubbed his fingers over the name and looked at Zeke in shock. Jamal still missed Nico, but maybe Zeke would actually understand how much he loved baseball. It was a lot to think about.

Zeke smiled, grabbed Jamal's glove and ball, and headed for home plate. "Yeah, M-Rod is from my old town! He's really nice. I met him in the park once and he showed me how to throw his famous curveball." Zeke stood behind home plate. "C'mon. Pitch to me. You use the M-Rod glove, and I'll use yours." He threw the ball to Jamal. "If you want, I can try to teach you what M-Rod showed me."

Jamal stood still for a second. Maybe when Nico came to visit, Jamal and Zeke could show him M-Rod's famous curveball. "Get ready!" Jamal called. He smiled widely as he rocked back, ready to fire the ball to his new friend.

textContent.text: Luca had loved art since he was old enough to walk. His parents hung all of his art on the walls. His friends begged him to paint characters from their favorite TV shows. But for some reason, he hadn't touched a paintbrush in weeks.
Lately, Luca hadn't felt like painting. His paints looked dull. He had drawn all of his friends' favorite characters in every pose he could think of.
One day after school, Luca went to the park with his friends. They ran and played while Luca stared down at his empty sketchbook. He thought and thought, but no ideas came to mind.
When his dad came to pick him up, Luca grinned and hopped in the car. His dad's car was his favorite place in the world. It was old, but well loved. It was covered in bright paint, inside and out.
Luca's dad turned to him as he got in the car. "Sorry, kiddo. I forgot something at the shop. We're taking the long way home today."

Luca didn't mind the detour. His dad was a mechanic and owned a shop downtown. Luca had spent a lot of time there when he was younger. In fact, watching his dad paint cars was where Luca first discovered his eye for color.
When they got downtown, the shop looked like it always did. The familiar sight made Luca curious.

pieces.text: Luca's dad ran into the office for his bag, but Luca spotted something in the garage. There was a newly painted car, covered with a swirl of bright colors. His eyes widened. He looked at the huge shelf of paint bottles. Each color was brighter than the next.

textContent.text: Luca ran into the office. "Dad! Do you think I am old enough to use the car paints? Could I try it?"

Dad grinned. "You know, I was just noticing my huge pile of scrap metal. We can't do a whole car, but I'll grab you a piece. Maybe it can be part of someone's car someday! Do you remember where the safety gear is?"
Luca bounced over to the cabinet for gloves and goggles. "Yes, I'm ready! I have so many ideas! Should I do a deep sea painting? Or maybe outer space?"
As Luca followed his dad back to the garage, he felt something he hadn't felt for weeks. Today, finally, he had a reason to paint.

textContent.text: Ezra McBride had big dreams. His father was a legend, known for finding gold where others found only dust and rocks. Ezra wanted to be just as good.
It was all he could talk about. Every free moment, he walked around the family's California ranch. He dug through dirt and even inspected the barn.
But Ezra's luck seemed as dry as the land around him.
One morning, as Ezra walked to the schoolhouse, a new girl ran up beside him. "My name's Jesse," she announced. "I just moved to town."
In her arms, Jesse carried a stack of maps and books. Ezra noticed that they were all about local rivers, hills, and mineral deposits.
Jesse continued, "I heard you like looking for gold. Want some help?"
Ezra shook his head. He didn't need help from someone who had only been here for a few days. His dad was the best miner around.

"I might just surprise you," Jesse said, grinning. "I may be new, but I've got a few ideas that might help you." Jesse opened a book and an old map. "It looks like a river used to run across your family's land. What if we try digging there?"
"Listen. I know my home better than you. You can search with me, but we do it my way."
Jesse shrugged. "I guess that's the way it's got to be," she said. After school, they walked along the dusty road toward the McBride farm.

In the days that followed, Ezra took them to a handful of promising spots. But time after time they uncovered nothing but rocks and dead bushes. Ezra started to wonder if he was being stubborn. Jesse's ideas couldn't be any worse than his.
One day, on the walk back from school, Ezra said. "Say, Jesse. Remember that old river you talked about? What do you say we give it a try?"
Jesse smiled at Ezra and nodded. "Yes!"

Hours later, Ezra spotted a few shiny flakes of gold right where Jesse thought they might be. Then, as he dug through more dirt, Ezra's heart beat faster. There were even small gold nuggets in the dirt.
He couldn't believe it. Jesse and her maps had guessed right.
Ezra leapt up. He grabbed Jesse's arms and spun them in a circle. "Jesse, you did it! You knew just where to look. We're going to be California legends, just like my dad!"
